Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) for <math>[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_n]^{2+}</math> and <math>[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_n]^{3+}</math> (<math>\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}</math> and <math>\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}</math> in liquid water), and for a water slab, are trained on the fly. This develops the procedure of Jinnouchi, Karsai, and Kresse {{Cite|jinnouchi:ncm:2024}}.

== Input files ==
=== {{FILE|POSCAR}}s ===
The following initial structures will be used in this example. Please run the calculations on each structure in a separate directory. The {{FILE|POSCAR}} files are described on more detail in the [[Thermodynamic integration: redox potential|redox potential overview page]].

=== {{FILE|KPOINTS}} ===
Only the &Gamma; point is used, so the {{FILE|KPOINTS}} file is:

 Gamma-point only
  0
 Monkhorst Pack
  1 1 1
  0 0 0

=== {{FILE|POTCAR}} ===
Standard {{FILE|POTCAR}} files are used throughout:
*<code>PAW_PBE H 15Jun2001</code>
*<code>PAW_PBE O 08Apr2002</code>
*<code>PAW_PBE Fe_sv 23Jul2007</code>

The water slab contains only H and O, so its {{FILE|POTCAR}} is built from the first two potentials only.

== Step-by-step instructions: Training of <math>[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_n]^{2+}</math> ==

=== Step 0: Preparing the calculation ===
Use the {{FILE|POSCAR}} for <math>[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_n]^{2+}</math>, {{FILE|KPOINTS}}, {{FILE|INCAR}} and {{FILE|POTCAR}} from this example.

=== Step 1: Determining the number of electrons of the neutral system ===
Execute the following command:

{{CB|mpirun -np 1 vasp_executable --dry-run|:}}

Using the [[Command-line arguments#--dry-run / -n|--dry-run]] argument, VASP executes most of the setup routines but bypasses the computationally heavy tasks. Besides testing the input, running VASP with this option is an easy way to determine system-dependent default values for tags such as {{TAG|NBANDS}}, etc. This run also determines the number of electrons {{TAG|NELECT}} of the system.
For that type:

{{CB|grep NELECT OUTCAR|:}}

You should get an output like:
   NELECT =     528.0000    total number of electrons

So the number of electrons in the system is 528. Use this value as a starting point for the {{FILE|INCAR}}.

=== Step 2: Running the on-the-fly training ===
First, train for {{TAG|NSW}}=50000 steps with a 1 femtosecond stepsize ({{TAG|POTIM}}=1.0).
Please run the calculation with the following {{FILE|INCAR}} file:

 {{TAGBL|NELECT}} = 526
  
 # Electronic parameters
 {{TAGBL|ENCUT}}  = 520.0 
 {{TAGBL|EDIFF}}  = 1E-5
 {{TAGBL|GGA}} = RP
 {{TAGBL|IVDW}} = 11
 {{TAGBL|ISMEAR}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|SIGMA}}  = 0.10
 {{TAGBL|PREC}}   = Normal
 {{TAGBL|LREAL}}  = A
 {{TAGBL|NELMIN}} = 4
 {{TAGBL|ALGO}} = All
 {{TAGBL|NELM}} = 200
 {{TAGBL|ISPIN}} = 2
 {{TAGBL|MAGMOM}} = 128*0 64*0 1*4
 {{TAGBL|NUPDOWN}} = 4
 {{TAGBL|IWAVPR}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|AMIX}} = 0.2
 
 # MD paramters
 {{TAGBL|IBRION}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|ISYM}}   = 0
 {{TAGBL|NSW}}    = 50000
 {{TAGBL|POTIM}}  = 1.0
 {{TAGBL|TEBEG}} = 300
 {{TAGBL|TEEND}} = 500
 {{TAGBL|MDALGO}} = 3
 {{TAGBL|ISIF}}   = 2
 {{TAGBL|LANGEVIN_GAMMA}} = 10.0 10.0 10.0
 {{TAGBL|LCHARG}} = .FALSE.
 {{TAGBL|LWAVE}} = .FALSE.
 
 # Machine learning
 {{TAGBL|ML_LMLFF}} = .TRUE.                    # switches on machine learning
 {{TAGBL|ML_MODE}} = train
 {{TAGBL|ML_MB}} = 6000
 {{TAGBL|ML_RCUT1}} = 6.0
 {{TAGBL|ML_RCUT2}} = 4.0
 
 # Parallelization for electronic calculation (depends on number of cores)
 {{TAGBL|NCORE}} = 4
 
 # Increase mass of hydrogen
 {{TAGBL|POMASS}} = 8.0 16.0 55.847
 
 # Set constant threshold for the Bayesian errors
 {{TAGBL|ML_ICRITERIA}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|ML_CTIFOR}} = 0.07

Since there are so many tags, they are described briefly below in the context of this system:
*{{TAG|NELECT}}: The previous step gave 528 electrons. To simulate <math>\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}</math> in liquid water, decrease the number of electrons in the system by setting {{TAG|NELECT}}=526 (the two electrons are put in the background to remain charge neutral in the SCF calculations). 
*{{TAG|IVDW}}: Van der Waals interactions are needed for water.
*{{TAG|ALGO}}=ALL: An "exact" solution of the electronic states is needed, since this system is set up as magnetic and, as with many of the magnetic systems, it can be hard to find global minima.
*{{TAG|NUPDOWN}}: Using this tag is absolutely necessary, since otherwise the magnetic states would strongly fluctuate, leading to very unfavorable configurations that cannot be converged electronically.
*{{TAG|MDALGO}}=3: Selects the [[Langevin thermostat]].
*{{TAG|ISIF}}=2: Runs the calculation in the [[NVT ensemble]].
*{{TAG|ML_MB}}=6000: Selects 6000 local reference configurations (4000 would likely also be sufficient). A larger number of local reference configurations leads to a higher accuracy of the force field but requires more computational resources and is potentially less stable.
*{{TAG|ML_RCUT1}}=6.0, {{TAG|ML_RCUT2}}=4.0: These are empirical settings for liquid water that lead to improved accuracy. 
*{{TAG|POMASS}}: The mass of hydrogen is increased by a factor of 8. The heavier hydrogen moves more slowly, which allows a larger time step. At its true mass, hydrogen travels a long way within one step while the heavier atoms barely move.
*{{TAG|ML_ICRITERIA}}=0: For complex systems, the automatic determination of the threshold for on-the-fly learning ({{TAG|ML_ICRITERIA}} = 1) can fail, so a constant threshold is used ({{TAG|ML_ICRITERIA}} = 0). Unfortunately, the threshold ({{TAG|ML_CTIFOR}}) is system-dependent, so it needs to be determined by the user via test calculations. 
*{{TAG|ML_CTIFOR}}=0.07: A value of 0.07 is a reasonable first choice for this system. It may need to be updated if problems are encountered during training.

=== Step 3: Continuing the training with a smaller threshold ===
Continue training for another {{TAG|NSW}}=50000 steps with a 1 femtosecond step size ({{TAG|POTIM}}=1.0).
Open a new folder in which you will continue the calculation; copy {{FILE|ML_ABN}} and {{FILE|CONTCAR}} from the previous folder to {{FILE|ML_AB}} and {{FILE|POSCAR}} in the new folder, respectively. Also copy the {{FILE|POTCAR}}, {{FILE|POSCAR}} and {{FILE|INCAR}} file to the new directory.

To further increase the sampling rate and the stability of the force field, decrease the threshold for learning in the {{FILE|INCAR}} file from 0.07 to 0.03:
 {{TAGBL|ML_CTIFOR}} = 0.03

After running the force field, obtain the errors of the force field on the training data by typing:

{{CB|grep ERR ML_LOGFILE|:}}

The exact errors are never fully reproducible, but one should have an error close to the following:
 # ERR ######################################################################
 # ERR This line contains the RMSEs of the predictions with respect to ab initio results for the training data.
 # ERR
 # ERR nstep ......... MD time step or input structure counter
 # ERR rmse_energy ... RMSE of energies (eV atom^-1)
 # ERR rmse_force .... RMSE of forces (eV Angst^-1)
 # ERR rmse_stress ... RMSE of stress (kB)
 # ERR ######################################################################
 # ERR               nstep      rmse_energy       rmse_force      rmse_stress
 # ERR                   2                3                4                5
 # ERR ######################################################################
 ...                 ...     ...              ...              ...
 ERR                 24182   3.34379956E-04   4.21034293E-02   3.25574507E-01
 ERR                 45641   3.52798835E-04   4.30397061E-02   3.24044663E-01
 ERR                 49316   3.72327940E-04   4.37625524E-02   3.18168785E-01

Typically a few percent deviation is expected, since the trajectories of the training runs cannot be reproduced if run in parallel (due to a random order of summation in MPI together with limited floating point accuracy). 
In the [[NVT ensemble]] the stress does not enter, so energy and force errors matter more. Accurate forces give a stable force field and a physically correct trajectory. Accurate energies matter because the force field is later used for thermodynamic integration, where the energy is the key quantity. An accuracy better than 0.5 meV/atom in the energy is sufficient here.

=== Step 4: Refitting ===
Refit the {{FILE|ML_ABN}} from the previous step and obtain the final {{FILE|ML_FF}} file.
For that use the following {{FILE|INCAR}} file that uses empirically optimized tags:

 {{TAGBL|ML_LMLFF}} = .TRUE.
 {{TAGBL|ML_MODE}} = REFIT
 
 {{TAGBL|ML_RCUT1}} = 6
 {{TAGBL|ML_RCUT2}} = 4
 {{TAGBL|ML_MRB1}} = 8
 {{TAGBL|ML_MRB2}} = 6
 {{TAGBL|ML_W1}} = 0.5

The final five tags have been empirically optimized for water. The most important change is the reduction of the cutoff radii: {{TAG|ML_RCUT1}} is lowered from its default value of 8 Å to 6 Å, and {{TAG|ML_RCUT2}} from 5 Å to 4 Å. Because a smaller cutoff radius also reduces the required descriptor space, the maximum numbers of radial basis functions, {{TAG|ML_MRB1}} and {{TAG|ML_MRB2}}, can be reduced accordingly. Collectively, these adjustments reduce overfitting, which is one reason this set of tags improves accuracy. The radial and angular descriptor mixing tag {{TAG|ML_W1}} has only a minor effect on force-field accuracy and is therefore not discussed here.

== Step-by-step instructions: Training of water slab ==

=== Step 0: Preparing the calculation ===
Use the {{FILE|POSCAR}} for <code>128H2O_slab</code>, {{FILE|KPOINTS}}, {{FILE|INCAR}} and {{FILE|POTCAR}} from this example.

=== Step 1: Running the on-the-fly training ===
The training of the slab works quite fine with an automatic threshold determination, so it is used in this example. For that, one does not need to set any tag explicitly, since that is the default.

Otherwise, the {{FILE|INCAR}} file for the water slab is similar to the previous examples:

 {{TAGBL|ENCUT}} = 520.0
 {{TAGBL|EDIFF}} = 1E-5
 {{TAGBL|GGA}} = RP
 {{TAGBL|IVDW}} = 11
 {{TAGBL|ISMEAR}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|SIGMA}} = 0.10
 {{TAGBL|PREC}} = Normal
 {{TAGBL|LREAL}} = A
 {{TAGBL|NELMIN}} = 4
 {{TAGBL|ALGO}} = Normal
 
 {{TAGBL|IBRION}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|ISYM}} = 0
 {{TAGBL|NSW}} = 50000
 {{TAGBL|POTIM}} = 1.0
 {{TAGBL|TEBEG}} = 300
 {{TAGBL|TEEND}} = 600
 {{TAGBL|MDALGO}} = 3
 {{TAGBL|ISIF}} = 2
 {{TAGBL|LANGEVIN_GAMMA}} = 10.0 10.0 10.0
 {{TAGBL|LCHARG}} = .FALSE.
 {{TAGBL|LWAVE}} = .FALSE.
 
 {{TAGBL|ML_LMLFF}} = .TRUE.                    # switches on machine learning
 {{TAGBL|ML_MODE}} = train
 {{TAGBL|ML_MB}} = 6000
 {{TAGBL|ML_RCUT1}} = 6.0
 {{TAGBL|ML_RCUT2}} = 4.0
 
 {{TAGBL|NCORE}} = 4
 
 {{TAGBL|POMASS}} = 8.0 16.0

For the slab, it is enough to train for 50000 MD steps, but running longer would further ensure the stability of the calculation.

After running the force field, obtain the errors of the force field on the training data by typing:

{{CB|grep ERR ML_LOGFILE|:}}

The exact errors are never fully reproducible, but one should have an error close to the following:
 # ERR ######################################################################
 # ERR This line contains the RMSEs of the predictions with respect to ab initio results for the training data.
 # ERR
 # ERR nstep ......... MD time step or input structure counter
 # ERR rmse_energy ... RMSE of energies (eV atom^-1)

=== Step 2: Refitting ===
Refit the {{FILE|ML_ABN}} from the previous step and obtain the final {{FILE|ML_FF}} file using the same {{FILE|INCAR}} as for the previous examples.

== Recommendations and advice ==
* The Bayesian errors and hence also their thresholds are system dependent. To determine {{TAG|ML_CTIFOR}} one could also first run a calculation with automatically determined thresholds, plot error predictions and thresholds at every MD step and deduce values for {{TAG|ML_CTIFOR}} from the plot.
* Let it be mentioned here that it is possible to increase the accuracy of the energy. This is achieved by increasing the weight of the energy equations during fitting using {{TAG|ML_WTOTEN}} (typically increase it to 5, 10 or even more). Of course at the same time forces and stress will become more inaccurate. So one needs to find a good balanced value where the increase in accuracy of the energy is significantly larger than the decrease in accuracy of the rest. The behavior with respect to {{TAG|ML_WTOTEN}} is unfortunately strongly system dependent. For this example, {{TAG|ML_WTOTEN}}=1 was good enough.
